mainTopic: Selling weapons and animals to non-Jews: shields, iron, broken animals, horses, fattened oxen, and wild animals (עבודה זרה ט״ז ע״א)
overview: The גמרא finishes its discussion of which war items may be sold to non-Jews. It rules like the יש אומרים that shields may be sold, limits רב אדא בר אהבה's ban on iron blocks to special Indian iron, and explains that weapons are sold nowadays to the Persians who protect us. Next it turns to the משנה's ban on selling large animals. רבי יהודה allows selling a broken animal, and the חכמים argue with him. בן בתירא allows selling a horse, רבי forbids it for two reasons, and רבי יוחנן rules like בן בתירא. The גמרא then asks about an ox being fattened for slaughter, tries a proof from a story about רבי's household, and rejects it. A new משנה forbids selling dangerous animals and helping build certain public structures. The גמרא brings רב's rule that a large wild animal counts as large livestock for selling, and starts answering a challenge from the משנה; that answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: If it could be avoided, it would be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the previous answer. Selling things that strengthen non-Jews would be forbidden if it could be avoided, but it cannot be.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it were possible to avoid it, indeed it would be forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: This short line finishes an answer that started on the previous page. Selling everyday goods like food also helps non-Jews, and if we could stop selling those, we would.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was why only certain war items are forbidden when food and other goods also make non-Jews stronger. The answer is practical: stopping all such sales is impossible without causing great harm and hostility. So the ban is limited to items like shields.

phrases.english: If it were possible, indeed it would be so.
phrases.notes: This finishes an answer from the previous page: if we could avoid selling them things like food without causing hostility, we would forbid that too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to a challenge raised on the previous page.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical necessity: the ban is limited because a wider ban is impossible.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anything that strengthens non-Jews, even food, should be forbidden to sell.
steps.terutzMaskana: In principle yes, but since it cannot be avoided, only special items like shields are forbidden.

steps.title: A second explanation of the shield argument
steps.stepSummary: Another version explains the argument about shields: one side says non-Jews kill with shields once their weapons run out, and the other says they run away instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: the reason shields may not be sold is that when their weapons run out, they kill with the shields. And the יש אומרים who say we may sell them shields hold that when their weapons run out, they flee.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different way to explain the argument about selling shields. Now the question is whether a shield is used to attack, not only to defend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, those who forbid shields see them as possible weapons, since soldiers fight with them when their swords are gone. The יש אומרים say that a soldier whose weapons are gone runs away and does not fight with his shield, so a shield is only for protection and may be sold.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (an opinion in the ברייתא)

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Shields, this is the reason they may not be sold:
because when their weapons are finished,
they kill with them.
And "some say: we sell them shields,"
because when their weapons are finished,
they flee.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different version of how to explain the argument about shields.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument is whether shields are used to kill (forbidden) or soldiers flee once their weapons are gone (permitted).

steps.title: The הלכה follows the יש אומרים
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, quoting רבה בר אבוה, rules like the יש אומרים, who allow selling shields.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: the הלכה follows the יש אומרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on shields: we follow the opinion that allows selling them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה accepts that a shield is mainly for protection, so selling it is not like selling a weapon. This settles the shield question.
steps.whatToRemember: Shields may be sold to non-Jews, because the הלכה follows the יש אומרים.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
The halakha is in accordance with "some say."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument explained in the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is permitted to sell shields to non-Jews.

steps.title: No selling blocks of iron
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה rules that blocks of iron may not be sold to non-Jews, because they hammer weapons out of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: we do not sell them blocks of iron. Why? Because they hammer weapons out of them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ruling: raw iron blocks are forbidden to sell, because they can be made into weapons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes beyond finished weapons. Even raw material is forbidden when its likely use is making weapons.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מוֹכְרִין לָהֶן עֲשָׁשִׁיּוֹת שֶׁל בַּרְזֶל,
phrases.english: We do not sell them blocks of iron.
What is the reason?
Because they hammer weapons out of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new related ruling about raw iron.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blocks of iron may not be sold to non-Jews, because weapons are forged from them.

steps.title: Then hoes and axes should be forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if iron is forbidden because weapons can be made from it, hoes and axes should be forbidden too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even hoes and axes should also be forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב אדא's reason. Tools are also made of iron and could be turned into weapons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If "could become a weapon" is enough to forbid, then almost every iron tool would be banned. That seems too broad, so the reason needs limiting.

phrases.english: If so,
even hoes and axes should also be forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ מָרֵי וַחֲצִינֵי נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אדא בר אהבה's reason that iron is forbidden because weapons can be forged from it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Tools like hoes and axes can also be made into weapons, yet they are sold, so the reason proves too much.

steps.title: It means Indian iron
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד answers that רב אדא was talking about Indian iron, a special kind of iron.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: this is about Indian iron.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד narrows the ruling. Only a special iron, the kind used for weapons, is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary iron is mostly used for tools, so selling it is fine. Indian iron is special and is meant for making weapons, so it is forbidden. This answers the challenge about hoes and axes.

keyTerms.meaning: Indian iron, a high-quality iron used for weapons

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:
It is about Indian iron.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 5 by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All iron blocks are forbidden, which would also forbid tools.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only Indian iron, which is used for weapons, is forbidden.

steps.title: But nowadays we do sell weapons
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a problem: nowadays Jews do sell weapons, so how is that allowed?
steps.simpleTranslation: And nowadays, when we do sell them weapons, how is that allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that current practice seems to go against these rules. This sets up רב אשי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything so far bans selling weapons, yet people in the גמרא's time were selling them. Either the practice is wrong or there is a reason it is allowed.

phrases.english: And nowadays, that we do sell them weapons,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets current practice against the ban on selling weapons.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ban on selling weapons and weapon material to non-Jews.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Jews sell weapons nowadays, which seems to go against the ban.

steps.title: We sell to the Persians who protect us
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that today's sales are to the Persians, who protect the Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: we sell to the Persians, who protect us.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי explains the current practice. The buyers are the Persians, who defend the Jewish community.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban exists so that we do not strengthen people who may harm us. When the buyers are the ones protecting us, that reason does not apply, so selling to them is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: Weapons may not be sold to non-Jews who might harm us, but they may be sold to those who protect us, such as the Persians in רב אשי's time.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
We sell to the Persians, who protect us.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: לְפָרְסָאֵי דְּמַגְּנוּ עִילָּוַון
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case: the buyers are our protectors.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Selling weapons today goes against the ban.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban does not apply when selling to those who protect us.

steps.title: רבי יהודה allows selling a broken animal
steps.stepSummary: Returning to the משנה's ban on selling calves and foals, the גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי יהודה allows selling a broken animal, since it cannot heal and live.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: calves and foals. It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יהודה allows selling a broken animal, because it cannot heal and live.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's words "calves and foals" and brings a ברייתא with רבי יהודה's lenient view on a broken animal. This opens a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on selling large animals depends on the non-Jew keeping and using the animal. רבי יהודה says a broken animal will not live long and will just be slaughtered, so the worry does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: Calves and foals (quoted from the משנה)

phrases.english: The mishna taught: "calves and foals."
It was taught: Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken animal,
because it is not able
to heal and to live.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲגָלִים וּסְיָיחִים. תַּנְיָא: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מַתִּיר בִּשְׁבוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה about selling animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה permits selling a broken animal, since it cannot heal and live.

steps.title: The חכמים: she can still give birth
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים argue that a broken animal can still be mated and give birth, so the non-Jew will keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: but they can mate her and she gives birth! And since they mate her and she gives birth, they will come to keep her.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים challenge רבי יהודה. Even a broken animal is useful for breeding, so the non-Jew will keep it around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה assumed a broken animal is useless and will be slaughtered right away. The חכמים say it still has value for breeding, so it will stay with the non-Jew and the usual worry comes back.

phrases.english: They said to him:
But don't they mate her, and she gives birth?
And since they mate her and she gives birth,
they will come to keep her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: וַהֲלֹא מַרְבִּיעִין עָלֶיהָ וְיוֹלֶדֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's reason in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's claim that a broken animal is useless and won't be kept.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The animal can still breed, so the non-Jew will keep it and the reason for the ban returns.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: when she gives birth
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה answers: when she actually gives birth, then the worry will apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: when she gives birth!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה stands by his view. He doubts that a broken animal really will give birth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's short answer means: show me that she gives birth, and then I will worry. He does not think a broken animal will actually breed.

phrases.english: He said to them:
When she gives birth!
phrases.notes: He means: once she really gives birth, then we can worry. Until then, there is nothing to worry about.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יהודה answers the חכמים' challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the claim behind the challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A broken animal can breed, so the non-Jew will keep it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A broken animal does not really breed, so the worry does not apply.

steps.title: So a broken animal cannot mate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes from רבי יהודה's answer that he holds a broken animal cannot accept a male.
steps.simpleTranslation: So apparently, she does not accept a male.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what stands behind רבי יהודה's answer. He holds that a broken animal cannot mate at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's "when she gives birth" only makes sense if mating is not possible for such an animal. That is the factual point the two sides disagree about.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה allows selling a broken animal because he holds it cannot mate. The חכמים forbid it because they hold it can still breed and will be kept.

phrases.english: Apparently, she does not accept a male.
phrases.notes: Both words in brackets mean "accepts." Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, and the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from רבי יהודה's answer in step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יהודה holds that a broken animal cannot mate, so it will not be kept for breeding and may be sold.

steps.title: בן בתירא allows selling a horse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that בן בתירא permits selling a horse, and brings a ברייתא with his reason: the work a horse does is not a Torah-level forbidden labor.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן בתירא permits selling a horse. A ברייתא teaches: בן בתירא permits a horse, because the work done with it is one that does not carry a חטאת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling of בן בתירא and then brings a ברייתא that explains his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We worry about selling large animals because the non-Jew will work them on שבת. A horse is mainly used for riding, and riding is not a Torah-level מלאכה that would require a חטאת. So according to בן בתירא there is no real problem.

keyTerms.meaning: A sin-offering, brought only for a Torah-level sin done by mistake
Work, especially work forbidden on שבת

phrases.english: Ben Beteira permits regarding a horse.
It was taught: Ben Beteira permits a horse,
because he does work with it
for which one is not liable to bring a sin-offering.
phrases.notes: He means riding, which is not a Torah-level labor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from רבי יהודה's broken animal to the next part of the משנה about horses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A horse may be sold to a non-Jew, because riding it is not a Torah-level forbidden labor.

steps.title: רבי forbids selling a horse for two reasons
steps.stepSummary: In the same ברייתא, רבי forbids selling a horse: it counts as a weapon, and it counts as a large work animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי forbids, for two reasons: one, because it has the status of a weapon; and one, because it has the status of a large animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings the other side: רבי forbids selling a horse and gives two separate reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is a new worry: a horse is used in war, so selling it is like selling weapons. The second reason puts the horse in the same group as other large animals that the משנה forbids selling.

keyTerms.meaning: A large animal, like an ox or donkey
The status of, the law of

phrases.english: And Rabbi prohibits
because of two things:
one, because of the status of a weapon,
and one, because of the status of a large animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A horse may not be sold to a non-Jew, both as a weapon and as a large animal.

steps.title: What does רבי mean by the large-animal reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands the weapon reason, but asks how the large-animal reason applies, since a horse is only ridden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that it has the status of a weapon, since it kills by knocking down. But what is the status of a large animal?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רבי's first reason but asks what his second reason could mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A horse trained for war really does kill, so calling it a weapon fits. But we just learned that a horse is used for riding, which is not a Torah-level labor. So why would the large-animal worry apply to it?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense that..., used before 'but' (אלא) raises a problem
What is it? What does it mean?

phrases.english: Granted, there is the status of a weapon,
since it kills by knocking down,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא תּוֹרַת בְּהֵמָה גַּסָּה מַאי הִיא?
phrases.english: but the status of a large animal, what is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the second reason רבי gave in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a horse, used only for riding, falls under the worry about large animals working on שבת.

steps.title: An old horse is used to grind
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains: when the horse gets old, the owner uses it to turn a millstone on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: When it gets old, he makes it grind with a millstone on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question by showing how a horse ends up doing real forbidden work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A young horse is ridden, but an old horse that can no longer go to war is put to work grinding grain. Grinding is a real Torah-level מלאכה, so the large-animal worry does apply in the end.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
When it gets old, he makes it grind with a millstone on Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An old horse is used for grinding, a real forbidden labor, so it belongs with large animals.

steps.title: The law follows בן בתירא
steps.stepSummary: Even after explaining רבי's reason, רבי יוחנן rules that the הלכה follows בן בתירא: a horse may be sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: The הלכה is like בן בתירא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the final ruling on the horse debate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Explaining an opinion is not the same as following it. רבי יוחנן explained רבי's reason, but in practice he rules like בן בתירא, so selling a horse to a non-Jew is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: Horse: בן בתירא permits selling it, since riding is not a Torah labor. רבי forbids it as a weapon and because an old horse grinds. The הלכה follows בן בתירא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יוחנן agrees with רבי just because he explained his reason. He explained it, then ruled against it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
The halakha is in accordance with ben Beteira.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הֲלָכָה כְּבֶן בְּתִירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining רבי's view, רבי יוחנן decides the law against it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is permitted to sell a horse to a non-Jew, like בן בתירא.

steps.title: What about an ox being fattened?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: what is the law for selling an ox that is being fattened for slaughter? The question applies both to רבי יהודה and to the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: what is the law of a fattener's ox? Ask it according to רבי יהודה, and ask it according to the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question and says it can be asked according to both sides of the broken-animal debate. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fattened ox right now is meant for slaughter, not work. The question is whether that makes it like רבי יהודה's broken animal, or whether it is still a work animal. The גמרא will explain why each side has room for doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked a question (a real doubt)
An ox being fattened for slaughter

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
An ox of a fattener, what is its law?
phrases.notes: An ox being fed heavily to be slaughtered for meat, not used for work.

phrases.english: Let it be asked according to Rabbi Yehuda,
let it be asked according to the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: שׁוֹר שֶׁל פַּטָּם מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the רבי יהודה / חכמים debate about a broken animal (steps 9-12).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether selling a fattened ox to a non-Jew is allowed or forbidden.

steps.title: Why the question exists for רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: Maybe רבי יהודה only permits a broken animal, which will never work. A fattened ox, if kept long enough, will become fit for work, so maybe it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Ask it according to רבי יהודה: maybe רבי יהודה only permits a broken animal, which will never come to work. But this one, which if he keeps it will come to work, is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the doubt according to רבי יהודה by giving the side that forbids it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's reason was that a broken animal will never work. A fattened ox is not working now, but if the non-Jew keeps it and stops fattening it, it can become a work animal. That difference might make it forbidden even for רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: He only permitted up to this point (and no further)
Keeps it, holds onto it over time

phrases.english: Let it be asked according to Rabbi Yehuda:

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָא שָׁרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda only permits
a broken animal,
which will not come to the category of work,
but this one, which when he keeps it
will come to the category of work, is forbidden.
phrases.notes: If he keeps it without fattening it, it can become a working ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּיבְּעֵי לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה: עַד כָּאן לָא קָא שָׁרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the first side of the doubt raised in step 18, according to רבי יהודה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי יהודה's permit for a broken animal stretches to a fattened ox that could later become a work animal.

steps.title: The other side: maybe even the רבנן permit a fattened ox
steps.stepSummary: The second side of the question: maybe even the רבנן only forbid a broken animal, which is not normally meant for slaughter, but they permit a fattened ox, which is normally meant for slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or maybe even the רבנן only forbid there, by an animal that is not normally meant for slaughter. But this ox, which is normally meant for slaughter, even the רבנן would permit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the question it started in Step 19 by giving the opposite possibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 suggested that even רבי יהודה might forbid a fattened ox, because one day it could work. Now the גמרא flips it: maybe even the stricter רבנן allow it, because a fattened ox is normally headed for slaughter, not for work. The case is left open, so the גמרא will look for a proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question)

phrases.english: Or perhaps, even according to the Rabbis,
they do not forbid there
phrases.notes: "There" means the broken animal from the earlier discussion.

phrases.english: except because it normally does not stand for slaughter,
but this one, which normally stands for slaughter,
even the Rabbis permit?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite side of the question begun in Step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the fact that a fattened ox is normally meant for slaughter make it permitted even for the רבנן?

steps.title: Story: רבי's household bribed their way out of giving a fattened ox
steps.stepSummary: A proof is brought from a story: the household of רבי had to give a fattened ox to the authorities on their festival, and they paid three bribes of forty thousand each to change and finally cancel this duty.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The household of רבי used to bring a fattened ox on the gentiles' festival day. They gave up forty thousand so that they would not bring it on that day but on the next day. They gave up another forty thousand so that they would not bring it alive but slaughtered. They gave up another forty thousand so that they would not bring it at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story as material for a proof. The actual argument from the story comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story describes three steps, each costing forty thousand: moving the gift to the next day, giving it slaughtered instead of alive, and finally not giving it at all. The fact that they wanted to avoid giving a live fattened ox looks like a hint that giving one is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox of a fattener; an ox fattened for slaughter

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
The household of Rabbi used to bring
a fattened ox on their festival day.
They lost forty thousand
phrases.notes: Literally "four ten-thousands." They paid this money to get the rule changed.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מַקְרִיבִין אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם אֶלָּא לְמָחָר,
phrases.english: so that they would not bring it that day, but the next day.
They lost forty thousand

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מַקְרִיבִין אוֹתוֹ חַי אֶלָּא שָׁחוּט,
phrases.english: so that they would not bring it alive, but slaughtered.
They lost forty thousand
so that they would not bring it at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story to try to answer the question of Steps 18-20.
steps.raayaObject: Whether giving a live fattened ox to a non-Jew is forbidden.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי's household, told by רב יהודה in the name of שמואל.

steps.title: The inference: they feared the ox would be kept for work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the reason for avoiding a live ox was the fear that the non-Jews would keep it until it was fit for work.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was the reason? Was it not because maybe they would come to keep it alive until it could work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the proof from the story: the reason they paid not to give it alive must be the worry that it would be kept and used for work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this is the reason, then a fattened ox is treated like a work animal, and selling it would be forbidden. That would answer the question of Step 18 on the strict side.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not because...? (a suggested reason)
To keep it alive, to delay

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Is it not because maybe they would come to keep it?
phrases.notes: He means keep it alive until it gets slim and can be put to work.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא, לָאו מִשּׁוּם דִּלְמָא אָתֵי לְשַׁהוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the story in Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: Selling a fattened ox is forbidden because it may be kept for work.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The bribe paid so as not to give the ox alive.

steps.title: Pushback: then why pay to move it to the next day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: the first bribe, to move the gift to the next day, has nothing to do with work, so the bribes must have a different reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: But by your reasoning, what was the reason for paying so that they would not bring it on that day, but the next day?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by pointing to the first bribe in the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving the gift from the festival day to the next day does nothing to stop the ox from being kept for work. So the worry about work cannot explain all the bribes, and the proof from the second bribe is weakened.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning (turns the argument back on the questioner)

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מַקְרִיבִין אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם אֶלָּא לְמָחָר —
phrases.english: that they would not bring it that day but the next day —
what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference of Step 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the story.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The work-animal reason cannot explain the first bribe, so it is not clearly the reason behind the bribes.

steps.title: The real reason: רבי wanted to end the practice slowly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי wanted to get rid of the practice completely, and he knew it was best to do so little by little.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי wanted to uproot the practice, and he thought: let it be uprooted, and it will happen little by little.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new explanation for the story, so the story no longer proves anything about selling a fattened ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three bribes were steps in one plan: to end the gift entirely, done in stages so the authorities would accept it. Since the reason was not the work-animal worry, the question of Step 18 stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: To uproot the matter, to end the practice

steps.whatToRemember: The story of רבי's household does not prove that selling a fattened ox is forbidden. רבי was simply ending a forced gift step by step.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi wanted to uproot the matter,
and he thought: let it be uprooted, and it will come little by little.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the rejection of Step 23 by giving a different reason for the story.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bribes showed a worry that a live fattened ox would be kept for work.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bribes were a step-by-step plan to end the gift completely, so no proof comes from them.

steps.title: Can a fattened ox really become fit for work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the idea from Step 19: if a fattened ox is kept alive, does it really become healthy enough to work?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if one keeps it, does it become healthy and do work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the idea that a fattened ox, if kept long enough, will be able to work, and asks whether that is true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole worry about a fattened ox depends on its becoming a work animal later. If a fattened ox can never become strong enough to work, the worry disappears.

phrases.english: And when one keeps it,
does it become healthy and do work?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מְשַׁהֵי לֵיהּ בָּרֵיא וְעָבֵיד מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the claim in Step 19 that a fattened ox can become fit for work.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a fattened ox that is kept alive can actually become a working animal.

steps.title: רב אשי: a kept young ox works twice as hard
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports from the expert זבידא that a young fattened ox, when kept, does double the work of other oxen.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: זבידא told me: A young ox, we keep it, and it does two for one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of Step 25 with an expert's report: yes, a kept fattened ox can work, and very well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the worry from Step 19 is real: a fattened ox can become a strong work animal. That is why selling it is a real question and not obviously allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: זבידא, an expert in raising cattle

steps.whatToRemember: A fattened ox that is kept alive can become an excellent work animal, so the worry about selling it to a non-Jew is real.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Zevida said to me:
A young ox, we keep it,
and it does two for one.
phrases.notes: It does twice the work of a regular ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אָמַר לִי זְבִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. A kept young fattened ox becomes fit for work and does double the work of other oxen.

steps.title: No selling dangerous animals to non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that we may not sell bears, lions, or anything that can harm the public to non-Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: You may not sell bears or lions to them, or anything else that can harm the public.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. Its first rule forbids selling dangerous animals, or anything that can hurt the public, to non-Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason given is danger to the public, not the fear of the animal being used for work, which was the reason in the earlier discussion about oxen. This wording, 'anything that can harm the public,' will soon be used to challenge רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה.' A new משנה starts here.
Harm to the public, danger to many people

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
One may not sell bears and lions to them
phrases.notes: 'Them' means non-Jews, the same people the earlier משניות were talking about.

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ נֶזֶק לָרַבִּים.
phrases.english: or anything that can cause harm to the public.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the discussion of the fattened ox ended with זבידא's report in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to sell non-Jews bears, lions, or anything that can harm the public.

steps.title: Which buildings one may or may not help build
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids helping build a basilica, a tribunal, a stadium, or a platform. It allows small structures and bathhouses, but not the dome where idols are placed.
steps.simpleTranslation: You may not build with them a basilica, a tribunal, a stadium, or a platform. But you may build with them small platforms and bathhouses. Once you reach the dome where they set up idols, it is forbidden to build.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second rule, about working with non-Jews on construction. Some buildings are forbidden, some are allowed, and even an allowed building becomes forbidden at the part made for idols.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists four public structures that a Jew may not help build, but it gives no reason here. Bathhouses are allowed. Even so, once the work reaches the dome where idols are set up, building it would directly help עבודה זרה, so the worker must stop there.

keyTerms.meaning: A tribunal or place of execution

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the same job can be allowed or forbidden depending on exactly which part of the building you are working on.

phrases.english: One may not build with them a basilica,
a tribunal, a stadium, or a platform,
but one may build with them
small platforms and bathhouses.
Once he reached the dome
in which they set up idols,
it is forbidden to build.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Helping non-Jews build a basilica, tribunal, stadium or platform is forbidden. Small platforms and bathhouses are allowed, except for the dome where idols are set up.

steps.title: רב: a large wild animal is like small livestock for the twitch test, but not for selling
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a חיה גסה is treated like בהמה דקה for the פירכוס test after slaughter, but not when it comes to selling it to non-Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב חנין בר רב חסדא said, and some say רב חנן בר רבא said, that רב said: A large wild animal is like small livestock for the twitch after slaughter, but not for selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב's rule about how to classify a large wild animal. It gets the 'small animal' rules for the sign of life after slaughter, but not for the rules of selling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier משנה said small livestock may be sold to non-Jews where that is the local custom, but large livestock may never be sold. רב says a large wild animal follows the small-animal rule for פירכוס, but for selling it is treated like large livestock, so selling it is always forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Small domesticated animals, like sheep and goats
The twitch or movement after slaughter that shows a weak animal was still alive

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two topics. פירכוס is about whether the slaughtered animal is kosher, and מכירה is about whether you may sell it to a non-Jew. רב treats the same animal differently for each one.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָנִין בַּר רַב חִסְדָּא,
phrases.english: Rav Chanin bar Rav Chisda said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא
phrases.english: and some say Rav Chanan bar Rava said
that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּה גַּסָּה הֲרֵי הִיא כִּבְהֵמָה דַּקָּה
phrases.english: A large wild animal is like small livestock
regarding the twitch after slaughter,
phrases.notes: A sickly animal is only kosher if it moves a bit after being slaughtered, which shows it was still alive.

phrases.english: but not regarding selling.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַיָּה גַּסָּה הֲרֵי הִיא כִּבְהֵמָה דַּקָּה לְפִירְכּוּס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא's first statement on the new משנה. It ties back to the earlier rules about selling animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חיה גסה counts as בהמה דקה for פירכוס, but as large livestock for selling, so it may not be sold to non-Jews.

steps.title: A second view: even for selling it is like small livestock
steps.stepSummary: The one who reported רב's words adds his own opinion: a large wild animal is like small livestock for selling too, so local custom decides.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I say: even for selling. In a place where people were used to selling, you may sell. Where they were not used to selling, you may not sell.
steps.whatsHappening: The person reporting רב's rule now gives his own view, which disagrees with רב about selling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב forbade selling a large wild animal in every place. This opinion treats it fully like small livestock, so the local custom decides, just as with sheep and goats in the earlier משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And I say,' the speaker giving his own opinion
A place where the custom was to...

phrases.english: And I say: even regarding selling,
phrases.notes: 'I' is the one passing on רב's words, here רב חנן בר רבא.

phrases.english: in a place where they were used to selling, one may sell;
where they were used to not selling, one may not sell.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the second half of רב's statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חיה גסה is like small livestock for selling as well, so it follows local custom.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from our משנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids selling bears and lions because they harm the public. That suggests a harmless wild animal may be sold, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: You may not sell them bears and lions, or anything that harms the public. The reason is that they harm the public. So something that does not harm the public is allowed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes our משנה and reads an implication out of it that clashes with רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives 'harm to the public' as the reason for the ban. So a wild animal that is not dangerous should be allowed to sell. But רב said a large wild animal can never be sold, so he seems to contradict the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But then,' introducing what follows from the reverse case

phrases.english: We learned in the משנה:
One may not sell bears and lions to them

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ נֶזֶק לָרַבִּים.
phrases.english: nor anything that can harm the public.
The reason is that it can harm the public,

phrases.aramaic: הָא לֵית בֵּיהּ נֶזֶק לָרַבִּים — שְׁרֵי!
phrases.english: so if it cannot harm the public, it is permitted!

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: אֵין מוֹכְרִין לָהֶן דּוּבִּין וַאֲרָיוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the משנה from step 27 to attack רב's rule in step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a חיה גסה may never be sold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's reason implies that a harmless wild animal may be sold. רב forbids selling it even when it is harmless.

steps.title: רבה בר עולא: the משנה is talking about a broken lion
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר עולא begins to answer that the משנה is talking about an injured lion. The answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר עולא said: It is talking about a broken lion,
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר עולא starts defending רב by saying the משנה is about a broken, injured lion. His explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An injured lion is not fit for work, so the usual reason for forbidding a sale (that the buyer will make it work) does not apply. The only reason left to forbid it is the danger to the public. So the משנה says nothing about a healthy large wild animal, and רב's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A broken or injured lion that cannot work

steps.confusionAlert: The amud ends in the middle of the answer. The full explanation of why a broken lion matters comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Ulla said:
It is about a broken lion,
phrases.notes: He means an injured lion that cannot be used for work.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר עוּלָּא: בַּאֲרִי שָׁבוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה is set in a narrower case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to allow selling any wild animal that is not dangerous.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a broken lion that is useless for work, so danger to the public is the only possible reason to forbid it. It teaches nothing about healthy animals.
